## merge vs rebase

**merge** — join two branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature
           \
            M  ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**rebase** — replay feature commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
             \
              D'--E'  ← replayed commits (new hashes)
```

---

## when use each

**merge when:**
- shared/public branch (never rewrite pushed commits)
- want preserve true history ("what actually happened")
- merging into `main`/`master`

**rebase when:**
- cleaning up local feature branch before PR
- want linear, readable history
- pulling latest main into your feature branch (`git pull --rebase`)

---

## tradeoffs

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| history | true, non-linear | clean, linear |
| commits | preserved | rewritten (new SHA) |
| conflicts | resolve once | resolve per commit |
| safe on public branch | ✅ | ❌ |
| bisect/log readability | harder | easier |

---

## golden rule

> **Never rebase public/shared branch.** Rewrites history = others' commits orphaned = pain.

---

## common pattern

```bash
# keep feature branch current (local only)
git checkout feature
git rebase main

# merge into main when done
git checkout main
git merge feature          # fast-forward if rebased
```

Rebase = clean history before share. Merge = safe join after share.
